osiLayers.name: Application
osiLayers.summary: Interface directly used by end-user applications for network communications.
osiLayers.details: Provides network services directly to software applications. Handles protocols like HTTP/HTTPS for web browsing, DNS for name resolution, and WebSockets for real-time bidirectional messaging.

osiLayers.name: Presentation
osiLayers.summary: Translates, formats, encrypts, and compresses data between network and application formats.
osiLayers.details: Ensures that data is in a usable format for the application layer. Handles TLS/SSL encryption and decryption, character encoding (UTF-8, ASCII), and data compression (gzip, brotli).

osiLayers.name: Session
osiLayers.summary: Establishes, manages, synchronizes, and terminates communication sessions between endpoints.
osiLayers.details: Maintains persistent dialogues between two devices, handling checkpoints, session recovery, and token management.

osiLayers.name: Transport
osiLayers.summary: End-to-end communication, error detection, flow control, and port addressing.
osiLayers.details: Responsible for logical communication between processes on host machines. Uses port numbers (0-65535). TCP provides reliable, ordered, byte-stream delivery with congestion control, while UDP provides fast, lightweight connectionless delivery.

osiLayers.name: Network
osiLayers.summary: Logical host addressing and packet routing across intermediate routers.
osiLayers.details: Routes packets across distinct networks from origin to destination using IP addresses. Determines optimal routing paths via algorithms like Dijkstra (OSPF) and Path Vector (BGP). Handles fragmentation and ICMP ping diagnostics.

osiLayers.name: Data Link
osiLayers.summary: Node-to-node frame transfer within the same local network using MAC addresses.
osiLayers.details: Transfers frames between adjacent nodes connected to the same physical link. Uses 48-bit hardware MAC addresses. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) resolves Layer 3 IP addresses to Layer 2 MAC addresses.

osiLayers.name: Physical
osiLayers.summary: Transmits raw, unstructured bit streams over physical transmission media.
osiLayers.details: Converts bits into electrical pulses, optical laser signals, or radio waves across physical cables, optical fiber, and wireless antennas.

transportProtocols.title: TCP vs UDP In-Depth Comparison
transportProtocols.summary: The fundamental divide in transport layer communication: Reliable Connection-Oriented vs Fast Connectionless.

tcp.name: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
features: Ordered Data Transfer (Sequence and Acknowledgement numbers)
Flow Control (Sliding Window prevents buffer overflow on receiver)
Congestion Control (Slow start, AIMD prevents network collapse)
Use Cases: Web browsing (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2), File Transfer (FTP), Email (SMTP), Database queries

udp.name: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
features: Unreliable / Best Effort (No ACKs, no retransmission of dropped packets)
No Ordering guarantees (Packets may arrive out of order)
No Congestion or Flow Control (Fixed, predictable overhead)
Minimal 8-byte header overhead (vs 20-60 byte TCP header)
Use Cases: Live Video Streaming, VoIP, Online Multiplayer Gaming, DNS queries, HTTP/3 (QUIC)

transportProtocols.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake & 4-Way Termination
transportProtocols.summary: How reliable connections are established and safely closed.
handshakeSteps: 1. SYN: Client sends SYN packet with Initial Sequence Number (ISN = X). State: SYN_SENT
2. SYN-ACK: Server responds with SYN (ISN = Y) and ACK (X + 1). State: SYN_RCVD
3. ACK: Client sends ACK (Y + 1). Connection is now ESTABLISHED.
terminationSteps: 1. FIN: Client sends FIN to indicate no more data to send. State: FIN_WAIT_1
2. ACK: Server acknowledges FIN. State: CLOSE_WAIT (Client moves to FIN_WAIT_2)
3. FIN: Server finishes sending pending data and sends its own FIN. State: LAST_ACK
4. ACK: Client sends ACK and enters TIME_WAIT (2MSL duration) before closing to ensure ACK was received.

dnsJourney.title: The Step-by-Step DNS Resolution Process
dnsJourney.summary: How typing 'google.com' in your browser resolves to an IP address (e.g. 142.250.190.46) in milliseconds.

steps.name: Browser & OS Cache Check
steps.desc: Browser checks its local DNS cache, then OS cache, then local /etc/hosts file. If found, resolution finishes in <1ms.

steps.name: Recursive DNS Resolver (ISP / 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8)
steps.desc: If cache misses, query travels to your configured recursive DNS resolver. The resolver checks its own cache.

steps.name: Root Nameserver (.)
steps.desc: The resolver queries one of the 13 global root server clusters, which directs the resolver to the Top-Level Domain (TLD) server for '.com'.

steps.name: TLD Nameserver (.com)
steps.desc: The .com TLD server replies with the Authoritative Nameservers for 'google.com'.

steps.name: Authoritative Nameserver (ns1.google.com)
steps.desc: The authoritative server holds the definitive DNS records (A / AAAA / CNAME) and returns the exact target IP address with a TTL (Time-To-Live).

steps.name: Cache & Connect
steps.desc: The resolver caches the IP and returns it to your browser. The browser initiates a TCP connection to the IP.

webProtocols.title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 (QUIC)
webProtocols.summary: The generational evolution of the World Wide Web's foundational application protocol.

items.details: Introduced persistent connections (Keep-Alive) and chunked transfer. Suffers from Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking on single TCP streams, requiring browsers to open 6 separate TCP connections per domain.
Switched from plaintext to binary framing. Introduced multiplexing (multiple parallel streams over a single TCP connection), header compression (HPACK), and server push.

Replaced TCP with QUIC over UDP. Eliminates TCP-level Head-of-Line blocking (packet loss on one stream does not stall other streams), provides zero-RTT connection resumption, and seamless connection migration across Wi-Fi and Cellular.

webProtocols.title: HTTPS & The TLS 1.3 Handshake
webProtocols.summary: How modern encryption secures web traffic against eavesdropping, tampering, and impersonation.
webProtocols.details: HTTPS runs HTTP over an encrypted TLS connection. Uses public-key asymmetric cryptography (RSA / Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) for initial mutual authentication and key exchange, then switches to ultra-fast AES-GCM symmetric encryption for data payloads. TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake to just 1-RTT (or 0-RTT for resumed sessions).

webProtocols.title: Real-time Web Communication: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets
webProtocols.summary: Comparing architectural mechanisms for live bidirectional and streaming web applications.

comparisons.mechanism: Client repeatedly requests endpoint every X seconds.
comparisons.overhead: Very High (Headers & TCP handshakes for empty data)

comparisons.mechanism: Server holds request open until new data arrives or timeout occurs.
comparisons.useCase: Basic chat notifications without WebSocket infrastructure

comparisons.mechanism: Persistent HTTP connection streaming unidirectional text/event data from server to client.
comparisons.useCase: Live sports scores, stock ticker, AI LLM token streaming

comparisons.mechanism: Full-duplex bidirectional communication channel established via an HTTP upgrade handshake.
comparisons.overhead: Extremely Low (2-byte framing overhead after connection)
comparisons.useCase: Multiplayer games, collaborative real-time editors, active trading terminals

proxiesAndLoadBalancing.title: Forward Proxy vs Reverse Proxy
proxiesAndLoadBalancing.summary: A forward proxy represents the client; a reverse proxy represents the server.
proxiesAndLoadBalancing.details: Forward Proxy: Sits in front of clients to route outbound traffic, hide client IP addresses, enforce company content policies, or bypass geolocation blocks. Reverse Proxy: Sits in front of backend web servers to route incoming traffic, terminate SSL/TLS, cache static responses, compress data, and balance load (e.g. Nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB).

proxiesAndLoadBalancing.title: Layer 4 (Transport) vs Layer 7 (Application) Load Balancing
proxiesAndLoadBalancing.summary: Routing decisions based on raw IP/Port vs inspecting application headers and URLs.
proxiesAndLoadBalancing.details: Layer 4 Load Balancer: Operates at Transport Layer (TCP/UDP). Routes traffic based strictly on source/destination IP and port numbers without decrypting or inspecting packet payloads (Ultra-fast, millions of packets/sec, e.g. AWS NLB, Linux IPVS). Layer 7 Load Balancer: Operates at Application Layer (HTTP/HTTPS). Inspects cookies, headers, URL paths, and query parameters to route requests to specific microservices (Smart routing, SSL termination, e.g. AWS ALB, Nginx, Envoy).

algorithms.name: Round Robin
algorithms.desc: Sequentially cycles through servers in order. Best when servers have identical specifications.

algorithms.name: Weighted Round Robin
algorithms.desc: Assigns weights to servers based on hardware capacity. Higher capacity nodes receive proportionally more requests.

algorithms.name: Least Connections
algorithms.desc: Routes traffic to the server currently handling the fewest active connections. Ideal for long-lived sessions (WebSockets, video streams).

algorithms.name: IP Hash
algorithms.desc: Hashes the client's IP address to determine the server. Guarantees a client consistently hits the same server for session caching.
